passages.text: MOUNTAIN, an eminence of land rising above the surrounding country.
Some philosophers suppose mountains to have been formed at the creation, together with the rest of the earth, and to have stood unchanged ever since.
Others ascribe them to the universal deluge, which, breaking up the crust of the earth, threw its fragments into heaps; and hence the shells found upon their tops.
The highest mountains in the world are the Andes of Peru, of which Chimborazo rises about 20,000 feet above the sea.
The great chains of mountains run for the most part from east to west.
Mountains are of great use in collecting the vapours of the atmosphere, which, condensing upon them, form springs and rivers.
A mountain is an elevated portion of the Earth's crust, generally with steep sides, that rises above the surrounding land.

Mountains are formed by tectonic forces, erosion or volcanism, which act over periods of up to tens of millions of years. Once mountain building stops, mountains are slowly worn down by weathering and erosion.
Most high mountain ranges, such as the Himalayas and the Alps, formed where tectonic plates collided and the crust was folded and pushed upwards.
Marine fossils found near mountain summits come from rocks that formed on the sea floor and were later raised by plate movements.

Mount Everest in the Himalayas, at 8,849 metres, is the highest mountain above sea level. Because the Earth bulges at the equator, the summit of Chimborazo in Ecuador is the point farthest from the Earth's centre.
Mountain ranges follow plate boundaries rather than any one direction: the Andes run north to south along the west of South America, while the Himalayas run roughly east to west.
Air forced up a mountain cools, and its moisture falls as rain or snow, which feeds rivers.

reasons: Rare terms appear in both: Chimborazo, Andes, shells on summits, springs and rivers.
Orogeny scores well on how mountains form but leaves out height and climate.

alignments.label: Unchanged since creation

britannica.quote: formed at the creation, together with the rest of the earth, and to have stood unchanged ever since

wikipedia.quote: act over periods of up to tens of millions of years

alignments.note: Mountains are still rising and wearing down. None is as old as the earth.

alignments.label: Heaped up by the deluge

britannica.quote: breaking up the crust of the earth, threw its fragments into heaps

wikipedia.quote: formed where tectonic plates collided and the crust was folded and pushed upwards

alignments.note: A sudden flood is replaced by slow collision of plates.

alignments.label: Shells on the tops

britannica.quote: and hence the shells found upon their tops

wikipedia.quote: come from rocks that formed on the sea floor and were later raised by plate movements

alignments.note: The shells are real. The sea did not rise to the summits; the sea floor rose to become them.

alignments.label: The highest mountains

britannica.quote: The highest mountains in the world are the Andes of Peru

wikipedia.quote: Mount Everest in the Himalayas, at 8,849 metres, is the highest mountain above sea level

alignments.note: The Himalayas had not been measured in 1778. One consolation: Chimborazo's summit is the farthest point from the earth's centre.

alignments.label: East to west

britannica.quote: run for the most part from east to west

wikipedia.quote: follow plate boundaries rather than any one direction

alignments.note: The Andes, which the entry calls the highest, run north to south.

alignments.label: Mountains make rivers

britannica.quote: collecting the vapours of the atmosphere, which, condensing upon them, form springs and rivers

wikipedia.quote: its moisture falls as rain or snow, which feeds rivers

alignments.note: Right: mountains catch moisture from the air and feed rivers.

alignments.label: Worn down

wikipedia.quote: mountains are slowly worn down by weathering and erosion

alignments.note: The 1778 entry has mountains standing unchanged.

suggestedQuestions: How did the 1778 entry explain the shells on mountain tops?
Which were the highest mountains in 1778?
What did the 1778 entry get right about mountains?

How did the 1778 entry explain the shell.answer: As a sign of the universal deluge, which broke up the earth's crust and heaped its fragments into mountains [B3]. Wikipedia says the shells come from rocks that formed on the sea floor and were later raised by the movement of tectonic plates [W4].

Which were the highest mountains in 1778.answer: The 1778 entry names the Andes, with Chimborazo at about 20,000 feet [B4]. Wikipedia gives Mount Everest in the Himalayas, at 8,849 metres, as the highest above sea level, though Chimborazo's summit is the point farthest from the Earth's centre [W5].

What did the 1778 entry get right about.answer: Two things: the definition [B1] [W1], and that mountains collect moisture from the air and feed rivers [B6] [W7]. Its accounts of how mountains formed [B2] [B3], which are highest [B4] and which way ranges run [B5] are all replaced in Wikipedia [W2] [W3] [W5] [W6].
